strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated problem: escaping local maxima in reward-guided diffusion sampling, and clearly frames prior work (Resampling, Zigzag Sampling, Search-over-Paths) within a unifying hill-climbing narrative via Figure 1, which aids intuition and situates the contribution well.

The proposed adaptive inversion depth mechanism is a sensible and relatively simple extension over fixed-depth search methods (e.g., SOP), and the algorithm is clearly specified (Algorithm 1) with sufficient technical detail (inversion operator, acceptance criterion) to support reproducibility.

Quantitative results are consistent across two benchmarks (Pick-a-Pic, DrawBench) and four metrics (HPSv2, AES, PickScore, ImageReward), showing Ctrl-Z Sampling outperforming DDIM, Resampling, Z-Sampling, and SOP with better NFE efficiency (7.6x vs. SOP's 10x) than the closest competitor.

The ablation studies are reasonably thorough, covering reward model choice, exploration initiation strategy, and the interaction between accept threshold and max search depth, which helps clarify design choices and demonstrates robustness of the method to different guidance signals.
Qualitative examples in Figure 3 are illustrative and support the claim of improved semantic alignment and global coherence over baselines.
weaknesses: Experiments are limited to a single base model (Stable Diffusion 2.1) and text-to-image generation only; despite claims of being 'model-agnostic' and broadly applicable across diffusion frameworks (also implied by video/3D/audio motivation in the introduction), no experiments validate generalization beyond this single U-Net T2I setting, which is a significant gap given the framing.

The reward model used for exploration guidance (ImageReward) overlaps substantially with one of the evaluation metrics (IR), raising concerns about reward hacking/self-serving bias in the primary quantitative comparison; while the paper acknowledges this and shows gains on other metrics, a more rigorous analysis (e.g., held-out human study) would strengthen the claims.

Comparisons focus only on sampling-time baselines from the same family (Resampling, Z-Sampling, SOP) at largely matched NFE budgets, but there is no comparison at equal compute against simply increasing CFG scale, more candidates in vanilla best-of-N with DDIM, or other test-time scaling baselines (e.g., particle/beam search methods mentioned in related work), leaving open whether gains are specific to the zigzag mechanism or simply from more compute spent via reward evaluation.

No human evaluation/user study is included despite the paper's claims of improved 'semantic alignment' and 'global consistency,' relying entirely on automated preference-model proxies that are known to be imperfect and potentially gameable.

The paper reports only average NFE overhead (7.6x) without variance/distribution details or wall-clock time, making it hard to assess worst-case cost or practicality for real deployment scenarios where tail latency matters.

The method has several hyperparameters (lambda, delta, dmax, N, Nb) whose sensitivity is only partially explored, and default settings (dmax = infinity) could in principle lead to unbounded worst-case computation for hard prompts, which is only briefly acknowledged as 'infrequent' without a rigorous cost-quality Pareto analysis across prompts.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and intuitive framing of diffusion sampling as hill-climbing and identifies a well-motivated gap in prior test-time exploration methods (fixed-depth/shallow perturbation strategies) versus the proposed adaptively deepening zigzag search.
The method (Ctrl-Z Sampling) is model-agnostic, requires no retraining, and is compatible with existing diffusion pipelines, which increases its practical applicability.

Experiments span two architecturally distinct backbones (U-Net-based SD2.1 and Transformer-based Hunyuan-DiT) and three benchmarks (Pick-a-Pic, DrawBench, T2I-CompBench), with four human-aligned metrics, providing reasonably broad empirical coverage.

Extensive and thoughtful ablations are provided (reward model choice, exploration initiation criteria, search depth/width scaling, acceptance threshold, exploration window), which strengthens the empirical case for the design choices and demonstrates a systematic understanding of the method's sensitivity to hyperparameters.

The paper reports NFE overhead transparently and compares against several relevant recent baselines (Resampling, Z-Sampling, SOP), rather than only against naive DDIM, giving a fairer sense of the method's cost-quality trade-off.
Qualitative examples support the claimed benefits in spatial relations, numeracy, color, and object binding, aligning with the quantitative CompBench gains.
Limitations (fixed acceptance threshold, lack of global reward scheduling, limited large-scale validation) are explicitly and specifically discussed rather than treated superficially.
weaknesses: Improvements over the strongest baseline (SOP) are often marginal or mixed on several metrics/benchmarks (e.g., Table 1 PickScore for SD2.1 is worse than SOP; AES gains are inconsistent as noted in the ablation section), and the paper's own analysis concedes numeracy and spatial-prompt cases where SOP is competitive or better, tempering the claimed general superiority.

All quantitative results appear to be single-run point estimates with no reported variance, confidence intervals, or statistical significance testing, which is a concern given that some metric differences (e.g., PickScore, AES) are small relative to plausible sampling noise from the stochastic reward-guided search.

The reward model used to both trigger exploration and evaluate candidates (ImageReward) is also very similar to the metrics used for evaluation (IR is literally one of the four reported metrics), raising a risk of a self-selection/optimization bias where the method is partly rewarded for optimizing the same signal used for evaluation; the CLIP-based/AES results, which are less directly tied to the reward model, show comparatively weaker or less consistent gains.

Experiments are restricted to relatively small/older base models (SD2.1, Hunyuan-DiT) at modest resolutions; scalability to larger, more modern text-to-image backbones (e.g., SDXL, DiT-XL/2, or flow-matching models) is not empirically validated, which the authors acknowledge but which limits confidence in generality.

The method introduces multiple additional hyperparameters (d_max, N, λ, δ) whose optimal settings appear benchmark/model-dependent (per the extensive ablations), suggesting practical tuning burden and possible sensitivity that is not fully resolved by the fixed defaults used in the main experiments.

The comparison of computational cost is reported only in terms of NFEs; wall-clock time, memory, or reward-model inference cost (which can be non-trivial, especially with parallel candidate evaluation) are not discussed, making the actual practical overhead less transparent.

No user study or large-scale human evaluation is included to corroborate the automated reward-based metrics, which is a common concern for text-to-image alignment claims since all reported metrics are themselves learned proxy models with known biases.
